claims: The U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) was established in 1772.
The U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) is one of the oldest federal law enforcement agencies.
The U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) acts as the security arm of the U.S. Postal Service.
Postal Inspectors are federal agents.
Postal Inspectors investigate over 200 federal crimes related to the mail.
Postal Inspectors investigate theft of mail and packages.
Postal Inspectors investigate mail fraud.
Postal Inspectors investigate identity theft.
Postal Inspectors stop illegal narcotics from being sent through the mailstream.
Postal Inspectors stop opioids from being sent through the mailstream.
Postal Inspectors stop other dangerous contraband from being sent through the mailstream.
Postal Inspectors protect postal employees from workplace violence and robberies.
Postal Inspectors protect postal facilities from workplace violence and robberies.
Postal Inspectors identify hazardous materials such as bombs or biohazards (e.g., anthrax).
Postal Inspectors handle hazardous materials such as bombs or biohazards (e.g., anthrax).
Postal Inspectors ensure the security of mail-in ballots during elections.
Postal Inspectors have authority to make arrests.
Postal Inspectors have authority to serve warrants.
Postal Inspectors have authority to carry firearms.
There are approximately 1,200 postal inspectors.
Postal Police Officers secure high-value facilities.
Postal Inspectors frequently work with the U.S. Attorney's Office.
Postal Inspectors frequently work with state law enforcement.
Postal Inspectors frequently work with local law enforcement.
The official website of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service is uspis.gov.
